cells.tense: There's a practice in your keeping right now, and the keeping is what has your attention.
cells.ask: Offer one finished piece of this work to someone who'll say plainly whether it holds
cells.core:
There are two things worth keeping in your care at once, and neither one is being starved — an hour for the practice, an hour for what waits on it, and both get what they need. You know the difference between tending something and clutching it, because the practice keeps teaching you that with how it feels on a given day.

The next thing wanting your care is a piece of this work that's done enough to be shown. Handing it over to someone who'll tell you the truth lets care move outward without you having to guard it. Honest eyes on the work return more than keeping it close ever does, and what comes back tends to be usable right away.
cells.sheetLine: You tend to what's growing, and you know two kinds of demand when you're holding both.
cells.verb: tending what's growing by giving it steady, careful form
cells.place: a practice of your own, kept up by repetition when no one is watching

cells.tense: A day that hasn't arrived yet has you rehearsing it while the one you're in goes untended.
cells.ask: Write down one outcome you're rehearsing and let today's session end without touching the list
cells.core:
A practice done because the day asked for it, not because some result is owed — the hour is kept, the rest that follows is full instead of restless, and more of it feels possible tomorrow. That's the ordinary shape of this working.

What's shifted is that the practice has stopped being the point; it's become the ramp to a picture you're chasing, and you're pushing at hours and outcomes no one has asked you for yet. The push costs you the ease that made the practice worth starting, and the reckoning you're braced for isn't coming. Whatever's growing here doesn't answer force; it answers being let alone between visits, and the picture you're straining toward stays out of reach exactly as long as it's being reached for.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering a practice you can't steer from ahead of it.

cells.tense: The keeping has gone thin, and the days keep passing while the practice stays where it was.
cells.ask: Today, do one small piece of the practice at whatever size you'd pick with no one watching, then write one line about how it went
cells.core:
On an ordinary evening a short, unimpressive session gets returned to — the same few minutes, nothing larger than the day can hold, and the low mood passes before the day does. The practice stays alive by being small enough that coming back is easy to choose, not by being impressive.

The hours have thinned out, and returning now feels like borrowing against a balance already spent. More effort on a practice that's gone quiet only pushes it further off, and the size of the return stops mattering once it's been made big. What brings it back is a reason small enough to meet today, kept standing because starting was chosen once and then honored, not because the whole thing got rebuilt.
cells.sheetLine: The practice thinned out, and what's needed is a small enough reason to begin again.
cells.verb: tending what's growing by giving it steady, careful form
cells.place: a practice of your own, kept up by repetition when no one is watching

cells.tense: You're already doing the work — the showing up, the keeping at it — and talking about it like something running on its own.
cells.ask: Name one practice as yours out loud, including what it costs you to keep it
cells.core:
A practice kept because it was chosen, not because it's a habit on autopilot — you know when it's feeding you and when you're just showing up out of momentum, and you can say so without dressing it up.

You keep calling it luck, or just something you do, while the effort stays constant and invisible. The work runs either way, but nothing credits it, and the person doing the keeping hasn't claimed it. Saying it's yours doesn't break the practice; it lets you see the cost of what you're already carrying, and finishing a piece of it feels like closing a door instead of losing ground.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping the practice alive and refusing to say you're the one keeping it.
cells.verb: tending what's growing by giving it steady, careful form
cells.place: a practice of your own, kept up by repetition when no one is watching
